question.prompt: An arithmetic sequence of positive integers has \(n \ge 3\) terms, initial term \(a,\) and common difference \(d \gt 1.\) Carl wrote down all the terms in this sequence correctly except for one term, which was off by \(1.\) The sum of the terms he wrote down was \(222.\) What is \(a + d + n?\)

solutions.title: Bound the length, then use divisibility
solutions.explanation:
A single error of \(1\) means the true sum is either \(221\) or \(223\). Factoring these nearby numbers will help determine the sequence length.

Let \(S\) be the true sum. The arithmetic-series formula gives
\[
S=na+\frac{n(n-1)}2d,
\qquad 2S=n\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).
\]
Because the terms are positive integers, \(a\ge1\); their common difference is an integer, so \(d>1\) means \(d\ge2\). Consequently,
\[
S\ge n+\frac{n(n-1)}2\cdot2=n^2.
\]
Since \(S\le223<15^2\), we have \(3\le n\le14\). Also, the factored expression for \(2S\) shows that \(n\) divides \(2S\).

If \(S=223\), then \(2S=446=2\cdot223\). The number \(223\) is prime: none of the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), which are all the primes below \(\sqrt{223}<15\), divides it. Thus \(446\) has no divisor between \(3\) and \(14\), ruling out this sum.

Therefore \(S=221\), and
\[
2S=442=2\cdot13\cdot17.
\]
Its only divisor between \(3\) and \(14\) is \(13\), so \(n=13\). Substitution gives
\[
442=13(2a+12d),
\qquad a+6d=17.
\]
Since \(a\ge1\), we have \(6d\le16\). Together with the integer condition \(d\ge2\), this forces \(d=2\), and then \(a=5\).

These values give a true sum of \(221\), consistent with a written sum of \(222\) after one term is increased by \(1\). Hence
\[
a+d+n=5+2+13=\boxed{20},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
